name: UNH/Durham Water Treatment Plant
use: Surface-water treatment plant for the jointly operated UNH-Durham water system (about 2 million gallons/day)
builtText: Operational March 13, 2020; replaced the 1935 Arthur Rollins Treatment Plant
style: Contemporary utility building with gabled roofs (from aerial)

facts.text: Became operational March 13, 2020, replacing the Arthur Rollins Treatment Plant built in 1935; UNH owns and operates it, including the Lamprey River pump station.
Treats water from the Lamprey River, the Oyster River or the Spruce Hole Well; maximum capacity about 2 million gallons per day; serves UNH and the Town of Durham.

Design-build by Woodard & Curran: a 26,000 sq ft plant with three residuals lagoons, a process area visible through interior windows, and a training lab for engineering students; sited above the 100-year floodplain beside College Woods, unlike the old plant.

verdict: The 2020 treatment plant serving campus and town: a tidy gabled utility building beside its lagoons.
notes: No licensed photo. Reference aerial: a long grey building with a gabled metal roof and stone-faced base, beside three lagoons and woods; tidy industrial architecture. Ceilings marked high because of the process hall (inferred, not documented). Square footage conflicts: a search snippet cited 41,800 sq ft from a 2017 UNH planning submission (not opened); Woodard & Curran says 26,000. Whether the old Rollins building was demolished is not confirmed.
judgeNotes: Aerial reference only. Scored as utility: high on condition and function, low on looks and story.
